opus-5.5.text:
I think compute changes the question from "can a machine ever do mathematics?" to "how should we spend a scarce resource to get the most mathematical insight?" Those are very different questions.

When people first hear about AI for math, they picture a huge model thinking very hard about the Riemann Hypothesis. But if you look at how progress actually happens, a lot of it comes from building a loop: the model proposes something, a formal verifier like Lean checks it, and the result feeds back into training. The verifier is the key piece. In most domains you can't easily tell if the model is right, so you pay for human evaluation or you guess. In formal mathematics, correctness is checkable, and checking is cheap compared to generating. That asymmetry is a gift. It means compute spent on search and self-play isn't wasted, because every verified proof becomes clean, trustworthy data.

So my view is that availability of compute should push us toward three things.

First, invest in verification infrastructure, not only bigger models. If you have more compute, the best use often isn't one giant forward pass. It's many attempts, each checked rigorously, with the successes distilled back into the model. Test-time compute plus a verifier scales in a way that pure pretraining on human-written math doesn't, because the amount of human-written formal math is tiny.

Second, be honest about where scale helps and where it doesn't. Brute-force search works well for competition-style problems with short, tightly scoped proofs. Research mathematics is different. The hard part is often finding the right definition, the right intermediate lemma, the right way to reframe the problem. Throwing more samples at a badly posed problem doesn't help much. So I'd use compute to explore structure: generating conjectures, testing them on many examples, building libraries of lemmas, and finding connections across fields that a single human wouldn't have time to read about.

Third, don't let compute concentration decide who gets to do mathematics. Historically, math has been one of the most democratic sciences. You need paper, a pencil, and a good idea. If the frontier of discovery requires a hundred-million-dollar cluster, that's a real loss. So I care about efficiency: smaller models that reason well, open formal libraries, tools mathematicians can run on a laptop and that work with them rather than replacing them.

The way I'd summarize it: compute is fuel, but the engine is the verifier and the feedback loop. If you design that loop well, every unit of compute compounds. If you don't, you're just generating a lot of confident-sounding text. And in mathematics, confident-sounding isn't good enough. It has to be true.

r001.rationale: The response discusses allocating scarce compute and distinguishes problem types, but does not say mathematicians’ intuition should guide that allocation.

r002.rationale: It recommends spending compute where it yields insight, but does not frame the amount allocated to a problem as an expression of mathematicians’ assessment of its importance.

r003.rationale: The response does not advocate using unlimited compute to solve every interesting problem; it emphasizes compute limits, efficiency, and problems where scale helps.

fable-5.1.text:
I think compute changes the question we should be asking. For a long time, mathematics was the one field where the bottleneck was almost purely human: you had a handful of people in the world who could hold a problem in their heads, and progress moved at the speed of their intuition. Now, for the first time, we can trade compute for exploration. That doesn't mean we should throw GPUs at every open problem and hope. It means we should be deliberate about where search actually helps.

The way I think about it, there are two very different kinds of mathematical work. One is verification and the other is discovery. Verification is where compute is almost unambiguously good. If you have a formal system like Lean, every unit of compute you spend produces something you can trust completely. You never have to re-check it. So in that regime, more compute just means more certified mathematics, and I'd argue we are badly under-investing there relative to the value.

Discovery is harder. Compute lets you generate enormous numbers of candidate conjectures, candidate proof paths, candidate constructions. But the thing that's scarce is not candidates, it's taste. Knowing which of a million directions is interesting is still something humans do much better than models, at least today. So if you have abundant compute, the right structure is a loop: let the machine explore very widely and very cheaply, formally check everything it produces, and then put human mathematicians at the point of selection and framing rather than at the point of grinding through cases.

What I worry about is the opposite failure, where people assume that because compute is available, mathematics will fall out automatically. It won't. Compute without a formal target becomes a lot of plausible-looking text. Compute without good problem selection becomes thousands of true but useless lemmas. The real leverage comes from pairing it with infrastructure, which is formal libraries, good benchmarks, and clean problem statements that a system can actually attack.

And honestly, I'd love to see mathematics treated the way we treat compute allocation in other sciences. We decide to spend a certain amount of search on the Riemann hypothesis the way an experimental physicist decides to allocate beam time. That's a very different culture from how math has historically operated, and I think getting there is as much a social shift as a technical one.

r001.rationale: The response says humans should select promising directions, but does not state that mathematicians’ intuition should guide allocation when compute is limited.

r002.rationale: It compares allocating search to the Riemann hypothesis with allocating beam time, but does not say that the allocation expresses mathematicians’ assessment of a problem’s importance under limited compute.

r003.rationale: The response rejects throwing GPUs at every open problem and argues for deliberate search and problem selection, rather than using effectively unlimited compute to solve every interesting problem humans can formulate.

astra-6.text:
I think compute should shape the strategy, but it shouldn’t define the ambition. When compute is limited, you have to be very deliberate about what you ask the model to do. Can it find a useful example or counterexample? Can it help isolate a lemma that makes the problem easier? Those can be valuable contributions without requiring an enormous search.

With more compute, you can explore more possibilities, but the question is how to turn that exploration into mathematical understanding. Searching a thousand approaches is useful only if you can recognize which results are correct and which ideas are worth developing. So verification and good feedback matter alongside scale.

I’d also want us to measure progress at different compute budgets. If an approach works only with resources that very few people have, that limits who can participate. Ideally, greater compute helps us discover methods that eventually make mathematical discovery more efficient and accessible.

r001.rationale: It says to be deliberate when compute is limited and gives possible tasks, but does not say mathematicians’ intuition should guide allocation among problems.

r002.rationale: It does not frame limited compute allocation as an expression of mathematicians’ assessment of a problem’s importance.

r003.rationale: It discusses exploring more with greater compute, but does not advocate using unlimited compute to solve every interesting problem humans can formulate.

sol-6.1.text:
I think compute should shape how we pursue mathematical discovery, but it shouldn’t define what we consider worth discovering. If you have more compute, you can explore more candidate proofs, test more conjectures, and generate more examples. But the challenge is still deciding which questions to ask and recognizing which patterns are meaningful.

I’d want a tight feedback loop: explore, check, and use what you learn to guide the next search. In mathematics, you can spend an enormous amount of effort pursuing an approach that simply isn’t going anywhere. So better judgment about where to allocate compute can matter as much as having more of it.

And I think the output should ideally help someone understand the mathematics. Finding a proof is wonderful, but finding a proof that reveals why something is true can open up a whole new set of questions.

r001.rationale: It says better judgment can guide where to allocate compute, but does not state that mathematicians’ intuition should allocate limited compute among mathematical problems.

r002.rationale: It does not frame compute allocated to a problem as expressing mathematicians’ assessment of that problem’s importance.

r003.rationale: It does not advocate using effectively unlimited compute to solve every interesting problem humans can formulate.
